abstract: Tea cultivar and growing altitude are key factors shaping tea quality. This study systematically investigated their individual and synergistic effects on the quality of fresh leaves of Zhongcha 108 (ZC108) and Fuyun 6 (FY6), which were collected at altitudes from 442 to 945 m. Chemical analysis revealed that ZC108 had higher levels of amino acids, theanine, sugars, flavonoids, and catechins than FY6. Increasing altitude reduced tea polyphenols, flavonoids, caffeine, and catechins in both cultivars. Non-targeted metabolomics identified 50 cultivar and 40 altitude-associated metabolites. Key metabolic pathways, including phenylpropanoid, purine, and flavonoid biosynthesis, were upregulated with increasing altitude. A significant cultivar × altitude interaction was observed for coumarin. Machine learning achieved 100 % accuracy in cultivar classification (RF: 96.7 %, SVM: 93.3 %, KNN: 90 %), highlighting the cultivar factors dominance. Key biomarkers, such as phenylethanol and 6-O-β-D-fructofuranosyl- d -glucose were identified. These findings provide a basis for tea cultivar identification, origin traceability, and quality control.

2.2
Preparation of samples
50 mg of the sample was weighed, and 1000 μL of the extraction solution containing the internal standard, 2-Chloro-
L
-phenylalanine, was added. The extraction solution consisted of methanol, acetonitrile, and water in a volume ratio of 2:2:1, with an internal standard concentration of 20 mg/L. The mixture was vortexed for 30 s, then steel balls were added and grinding was performed at 45 Hz for 10 min. This was followed by ultrasonic treatment for 10 min in an ice water bath. The samples were centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 15 min at 4 °C. 500 μL of the supernatant was carefully transferred into an EP tube, and the extract was dried using a vacuum concentrator. To the dried solid, 160 μL of the extract, maintaining an acetonitrile to water volume ratio of 1:1, was added for re-dissolution. Vortexing was done for 30 s, and ultrasonic treatment was performed in an ice water bath for an additional 10 min (
Lv et al., 2024
). The sample was centrifuged again at 4 °C at 12,000 rpm for 15 min. Finally, 120 μL of the supernatant was carefully transferred into a 2 mL injection vial for HPLC, UHPLC-QTOF-MS analysis, and determination of TP and total flavonoids.
0.5 g of the ground sample (accurate to 0.0001 g) was weighed, then 40 mL of boiling water was added. The mixture was extracted in a boiling water bath for 30 min and filtered immediately. The residue was washed several times with boiling water, the filtrates were combined, and water was added to achieve a final volume of 250 mL. It was shaken well and set aside for the determination of free amino acids and total soluble sugars.
2.3
Determination of main chemical components in tea
The content of TP in the samples was estimated using the Folin-Ciocalteu colorimetric method, with GA as the standard (
Wang, Peng, & Gong, 2011
).The total free amino acid content was determined by the ninhydrin colorimetric method, using theanine as the standard (
Gao et al., 2019
). Theanine content was measured through high-performance liquid chromatography, following the national standard GB/T 23193–2017. The phenol-ammonia ratio was calculated as the ratio of TP to total amino acids. Total flavonoids were analyzed using the aluminum trichloride‑sodium nitrite colorimetric method, with rutin as the standard (
Liu et al., 2018
). The resulting regression equation is y = 1.1657× + 0.0306 (R
2
= 0.9998). The soluble sugar content was determined by anthrone colorimetry, using glucose as the standard (
Ying et al., 2020
). The resulting regression equation is y = 0.0028× + 0.085 (R
2
= 0.9982).
2.4
Determination of minerals
Accurately weighed 0.1 g (with a precision of 0.0001 g) of the tea leaf sample. Ground it uniformly and placed it into a digestion vessel. Added 10 mL of nitric acid, covered the vessel, and let it stand for 30 min. The vessel lid was securely tightened and digestion was performed according to the standard operating procedures of the Microwave Digestion System (CEM MARS 6, CEM Corporation, USA). Anabolism procedure: heated to 120 °C over 12 min and hold for 3 min, then increased to 150 °C over 5 min and hold for 5 min, finally, raised the temperature to 180 °C over 5 min and hold for 40 min. After cooling, removed the digestion vessel and slowly opened the lid to vent. The inner lid was rinsed with a small amount of water, and then the digestion vessel was placed on a temperature-controlled hot plate. Heated at 180 °C for 30 min, diluted the solution to 25 mL with water, mixed thoroughly, and set aside. Conducted a blank test simultaneously. The blank solution and sample solution were injected separately into the Inductively Coupled Optical Emission Spectrometer (Agilent 5110 VDV, Agilent Corporation, USA) to measure the signal response values of the target and internal standard elements, and the detection wavelengths for each mineral element were shown in Table S1. The concentration of the target elements in the digestion solution was determined based on the standard curve.
2.5
UPLC-QTOF-MS-based metabolomics analysis
The liquid-mass spectrometry system for metabolomics analysis comprised a Waters Acquity I-Class PLUS ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography (UHPLC) system in tandem with a Waters Xevo G2-XS QTOF high-resolution mass spectrometer (Waters Corporation, USA). Chromatographic separation was performed on a Waters Acquity HSS T3 column (2.1 × 100 mm, 1.8 μm, Waters, U.S.A.) at 40 °C. The mobile phases were as follows: Phase A consisted of ultrapure water with 0.1 % formic acid, while Phase B was acetonitrile with 0.1 % formic acid. The flow rate was set at 0.4 mL/min, and the gradient elution program was implemented as follows: 0–0.5 min, 5 % B; 0.5–5.5 min, 5–50 % B; 5.5–9.0 min, 50–95 % B; and 9.0–10.5 min, 95 % B, 10.5–12.0 min, 5 % B. The separation was carried out at 40 °C. The injection volume was 2 μL, and the autosampler temperature was maintained at 4 °C (
Dan et al., 2022
). In this experiment, MSe mode was employed for the acquisition of primary and secondary mass spectrometry data in both positive and negative ionization modes (ESI+ and ESI-). The acquisition range was set between 50 and 1200 Da, allowing for simultaneous dual-channel data acquisition at both low and high collision energies during each data acquisition cycle. The low collision energy was disabled, while the high collision energy was maintained within an interval of 10–40 V, with a scan time of 0.2 s. The parameters for the ESI ion source were as follows: capillary voltage of 2500 V (ESI+) and − 2000 V (ESI-), cone voltage of 30 V, and an ion source temperature of 100 °C (
Sun et al., 2022
). To monitor system stability and ensure the accuracy of the data obtained through the developed method, quality control (QC) samples were injected at intervals of every 10 samples. The raw data acquired using MassLynx V4.2 were processed for operations such as peak extraction and peak alignment using Progenesis QI software. After importing the raw data, a QC sample was selected as the reference for automatic peak picking and retention time alignment to correct for instrumental drift. The minimum intensity threshold for peak detection was set to 1000 counts. The intensities of the aligned compounds were then normalized against the total ion intensity of all compounds in each sample. In the resulting data matrix, any missing values were imputed with one-fifth of the minimum value of the corresponding compound within its specific group. Finally, compounds that were detectable in at least 80 % of the samples in any group were retained for subsequent statistical analysis. Identification was conducted based on the Progenesis QI software's online METLIN database, public databases, as well as self-constructed libraries, while theoretical fragmentation identification was performed concurrently (
Wang et al., 2016
).
2.6
Chemometrics analysis
Following the feasibility assessment of the non-targeted metabolomics data by the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) test and Bartlett's test, principal component analysis (PCA), partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA), and orthogonal partial least squares discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA) were conducted using SIMCA 14.1 software. The variable importance in projection (VIP) of predictor variables was calculated. Permutation test (
n
= 200) and cross-validation were employed to prevent overfitting and to ensure the reliability of the supervised results. Additionally, a
t
-test was performed using SPSS 27.0 software to calculate the
p
-values for significant differences among each compound. Differential metabolites were identified under the criteria of
P
< 0.05 and VIP ≥ 1 (
Xiao et al., 2022
). Machine learning was conducted using software packages in R version 4.4.2. The test samples were divided in a 7:3 ratio, with 70 % of the samples designated as the training set and 30 % as the test set. A 5-fold cross-validation approach was adopted to ensure the stability of the algorithm. The performance of the machine learning algorithm was evaluated using a confusion matrix, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, and area under the curve (AUC) (
Li, Elliott, Petchkongkaew, & Wu, 2024
). Support Vector Machine (SVM) was a supervised learning algorithm that performed classification by constructing optimal hyperplanes in feature space (
Mohammadi, Esteki, & Simal-Gandara, 2024
). In this study, SVM were constructed using a linear kernel function. K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) was a supervised machine learning algorithm that utilized a distance metric to classify samples based on their proximity to neighboring samples in feature space (
Li, Onoda, & Kumazaki, 2017
). In this study, K = 9 was determined to be the optimal value through the optimization of multiple tests. Random Forest (RF) is a supervised machine learning algorithm used for classification predictions. It integrated multiple decision trees by employing bagging and random feature selection (
Breiman, 2001
). The study utilized 400 random forests to achieve optimal discrimination. Discrimination models for variety and elevation were established using Support Vector Machine (SVM), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), and Random Forest (RF) methods.
2.7
Statistical analysis
All sample were conducted in triplicate. Data were analyzed using SPSS 27.0 (SPSS Inc., Chicago, USA). Statistical significance (
P
< 0.05) was determined by one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), the interaction effects were analyzed by two-way ANOVA, with different superscript letters indicating significant differences among means.

1
Introduction
Tea, the world's most popular non-alcoholic beverage (
Li et al., 2021
), derive its unique flavor and health benefits from a rich profile of bioactive components, including amino acids, tea polyphenols (TP), polysaccharides, and others (
Liao, Fu, Zeng, & Yang, 2022
). The biosynthesis of these compounds is significantly influenced by factors such as cultivar and environmental conditions. The interplay between genetic traits and environmental factors ultimately shape the distinct qualities of tea (
Wang, Cheng, Cheng, Li, & Huang, 2023
).
The tea cultivar, serving as the genetic foundation, fundamentally determine inherent differences in metabolic pathways. Tens of thousands of differentially expressed genes may exist between distinct cultivars, resulting in the upregulation or downregulation of various genes within common pathways involved in internal compound metabolism (
Guo et al., 2019
). Consequently, teas processed from different cultivars exhibit variations in their internal compound profiles, leading to differences in flavor and health benefits (
Cai et al., 2025
). Numerous studies demonstrated that cultivar differences could induce the upregulation of structural genes (CHS, F3H), thereby promoting the biosynthesis of flavonoids such as quercetin glycosides (
Yue et al., 2022
). Albino tea cultivars, harboring mutations in the CsPOR gene, exhibited defective chlorophyll synthesis. Concurrently, CsMYB4 acted as a negative regulator of the catechin pathway, reducing epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG) content. High-caffeine cultivars carried allelic variations, such as in CsTIDH, which enhanced purine alkaloid synthesis (
Kong et al., 2025
). Additionally, the differential accumulation of mineral elements (Se, Fe, Mg, K) from the soil among different cultivars also significantly impacted tea quality (
Cai et al., 2025
).
Altitude serves as a critical environmental variable. Variations along its gradient cause synchronous fluctuations in light intensity, temperature, humidity, and atmospheric pressure. These co-varying factors are major causes of differences in quality and physicochemical composition between fresh tea leaves and processed tea. Within a certain altitudinal range, increasing altitude exerted a favorable regulatory effect on the growth and development of tea plants (
Wen-Yan et al., 2017
). The lower temperature in high-altitude areas slowed down the growth rate of tea leaves and prolonged the growth cycle. This facilitated more thorough nutrient accumulation, leading to more complex profiles of internal compounds and consequently richer aroma and taste profiles in the tea (
Wang et al., 2022
). A previous study has found that as altitude increased, the amino acid content in tea leaves showed a statistically significant linear increase, while the content of TP and the phenol ammonia acid exhibited statistically significant exponential decreases (
Zeng, Zhou, Liao, & Yang, 2021
). However, currently, most studies have examined the impact of individual factors on tea quality in isolation, while few have investigated the relative contributions of multiple factors to tea quality. Although some studies have explored the effects of elevation and soil characteristics on tea leaves, and found that elevation was positively correlated with the amino acid content of tea leaves, and flavonoid content was positively correlated with soil total phosphorus and total sulfur of the soil, which provided a preliminary basis for the influence of how environmental factors influenced the quality of fresh leaves (
Ran et al., 2023
). Nevertheless, the interaction between tea varieties and altitude remains an underexplored area.
ZC108 and FY6 cultivars were widely cultivated in agricultural production and were known to possess distinctly contrasting metabolic phenotypes. ZC108 was typically characterized by a fresh and brisk taste (
Duan et al., 2014
), while FY6 was known for its mellow and robust flavor (
Zhu et al., 2018
). This clear difference made them ideal for studying how cultivars affect tea quality. Accordingly, in the present study, we selected ZC108 and FY6 as research objects, systematically measured the key physicochemical indices of fresh leaf samples collected from different altitude gradients, and explored effects of cultivar and altitude gradient on critical physicochemical indicators in fresh leaves. By employed non-targeted metabolomics to overcome the limitations of traditional methods, a wide range of small-molecule metabolites in tea leaves could be detected in an unbiased manner. Combined with machine learning, non-targeted metabolomic data were efficiently analyzed to identify key metabolites in tea cultivars and altitude ranges. Finally, the predictive accuracy of the model was used to determine the dominant factors affecting quality. We hope our results could demonstrate that integrating non-targeted metabolomics and machine learning could not only identify the key metabolites for distinguishing tea cultivars and altitudes, but also further reveal the contribution of genetic and environmental factors in shaping the metabolic basis of tea quality, thus providing a certain scientific basis for precise tea plant breeding and cultivation zoning in the future.

< 0.05 and VIP ≥ 1 (
Xiao et al., 2022
). Machine learning was conducted using software packages in R version 4.4.2. The test samples were divided in a 7:3 ratio, with 70 % of the samples designated as the training set and 30 % as the test set. A 5-fold cross-validation approach was adopted to ensure the stability of the algorithm. The performance of the machine learning algorithm was evaluated using a confusion matrix, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, and area under the curve (AUC) (
Li, Elliott, Petchkongkaew, & Wu, 2024
). Support Vector Machine (SVM) was a supervised learning algorithm that performed classification by constructing optimal hyperplanes in feature space (
Mohammadi, Esteki, & Simal-Gandara, 2024
). In this study, SVM were constructed using a linear kernel function. K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) was a supervised machine learning algorithm that utilized a distance metric to classify samples based on their proximity to neighboring samples in feature space (
Li, Onoda, & Kumazaki, 2017
). In this study, K = 9 was determined to be the optimal value through the optimization of multiple tests. Random Forest (RF) is a supervised machine learning algorithm used for classification predictions. It integrated multiple decision trees by employing bagging and random feature selection (
Breiman, 2001
). The study utilized 400 random forests to achieve optimal discrimination. Discrimination models for variety and elevation were established using Support Vector Machine (SVM), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), and Random Forest (RF) methods.
2.7
Statistical analysis
All sample were conducted in triplicate. Data were analyzed using SPSS 27.0 (SPSS Inc., Chicago, USA). Statistical significance (
P
< 0.05) was determined by one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), the interaction effects were analyzed by two-way ANOVA, with different superscript letters indicating significant differences among means.
3
Results and discussions
3.1
Analysis of the correlation between altitude gradient and cultivar on the internal composition of tea leaves
3.1.1
Analysis of the main chemical composition
TP was key contributors to the color, aroma and flavor of tea, and they represented the most significant functional components of tea (
Ma et al., 2025
). As shown in
Fig. 1
A, within the same altitude range, the content of TP in FY6 was generally higher than that in ZC108. It was hypothesized that FY6 possessed a stronger astringency and a more robust flavor. As altitude increased, the tea polyphenols content in both FY6 and ZC108 exhibited a declining trend, that the content in FY6 declining from 20.64 % to 19.90 %, and in ZC108 decreasing from 19.86 % to 19.63 %. This decrease might be attributed to the low-temperature environment at high altitudes, which inhibited the activity of key enzymes (phenylalanine ammonia-lyase, PAL) responsible for synthesizing tea polyphenols in the tea plant, resulting in the reduced accumulation of TP (
Mamati, Liang, & Lu, 2006
).

Physicochemical properties of Fuyun 6 and Zhongcha108 at low and high altitudes. Total tea polyphenols (A). Total free amino acids (B). Phenol ammonia (C). Soluble sugar (D). Total flavonoids (E). Note: data are presented as means ± standard deviation (

= 3). Different lowercase letters indicated significant differences set at

Amino acids imparted fresh and sweet flavor to tea, effectively mitigating the bitter and astringent sensations caused by compounds such as TP and CAF (
Zhang et al., 2019
). Among these amino acids, theanine was particularly notable, as it constituted the largest proportion of free amino acids in tea. Theanine contributed to the formation of tea's distinctive refreshing taste and provided various health benefits, including neuroprotective and anxiolytic effects (
Li et al., 2021
). It was a secondary metabolite with significant activity in tea plants. As illustrated in
Fig. 1
B-C, ZC108 exhibited significantly higher levels of both total free amino acids and theanine compared to FY6 within the same altitude range (
P
< 0.05), with the total free amino acids rising from 5.69 % to 6.66 % and theanine from 2.02 % to 2.97 %. As altitude increased, the total free amino acids and theanine exhibited a significant increase in FY6 (
P
< 0.05), and ZC108 displayed an upward trend in these components, although the changes were not statistically significant (
P >
0.05). Overall, the free amino acid content in both varieties was higher in high-altitude areas compared to low-altitude regions. This phenomenon was primarily attributed to the lower temperatures, abundant precipitation, and higher organic matter content in the soil found in high-altitude areas. These conditions optimized the nitrogen metabolism pathways of tea trees, thereby promoting the accumulation of amino acids (
Zhang, Ni, Long, & Ruan, 2023
).
The phenol ammonia, which represented the proportion of TP to amino acids in tea, was a crucial indicator for assessing the taste and quality of tea. A high phenol ammonia resulted in a bitter and astringent flavor, whereas a low ratio yielded a fresh and mellow taste (
Liang, Zhang, Ma, Zeng, & Fang, 2023
). As shown in
Fig. 1
D, within the same altitude range, the phenol ammonia of ZC108 was generally lower than that of FY6. Specifically, at altitudes below 700 m, the phenol ammonia of ZC108 (2.80) was significantly lower than that of FY6 (3.67) (
P
< 0.05), indicating that the tea soup of ZC108 was more refreshing and sweet. As altitude increased, the content of TP in both FY6 and ZC108 decreased, while the concentration of free amino acids increased. Consequently, the phenol ammonia diminished. It was hypothesized that both FY6 and ZC108 exhibited a sweeter and more refreshing profile in high-altitude regions.
Soluble sugar, an important metabolite that influenced the flavor quality of tea (
Shevchuk, Megias-Perez, Zemedie, & Kuhnert, 2020
), not only directly contributed to the sweetness of the tea soup, but also served as a substrate for the maillard reaction, which generated aromatic compounds in tea (
Mao et al., 2018
). As shown in
Fig. 1
E, within the same altitude range, the soluble sugar content of ZC108 was generally higher than that of FY6. This suggested that the sweetness of ZC108 was superior to that of FY6, which aligned with its lower phenol ammonia. Additionally, the soluble sugar content increased from 2.93 % to 3.14 % in FY6 and from 3.04 % to 3.19 % in ZC108 as altitude increased, indicating that these varieties were sweeter in high-altitude regions. This finding was further supported by experimental results demonstrating that the phenol ammonia ratio of both varieties decreased under high-altitude conditions.
Total flavonoids, which included flavonols and flavonoid glycosides, significantly influenced the color of tea soup and exhibited strong antioxidant properties (
Yue et al., 2019
). As shown in
Fig. 1
F, within the same altitude range, the total flavonoid content of ZC108 was generally higher than that of FY6, with a particularly significant difference observed at altitudes below 700 m (
P
< 0.05). At these altitudes, the Total flavonoids of ZC108 were measured at 0.98 %, compared to 0.74 % for FY6. As altitude increased, the total flavonoid content of both FY6 and ZC108 exhibited a decreasing trend. This decline might be attributed to the fact that the synthesis of the flavonoid skeleton relied on flavonol synthase (FLS), and the optimal temperature for the activity of this enzyme was 25–30 °C. The temperature in high-altitude areas was relatively low, which inhibited the enzyme activity, thereby inhibiting the synthesis of flavonoids (
Singh et al., 2008
).
In summary, the contents of total free amino acids, theanine, soluble sugar, and total flavonoids in ZC108 were higher than those in FY6 within the same altitude range, whereas tea polyphenols and phenol ammonia were more abundant in FY6. As altitude increased, the levels of total free amino acids, theanine, and soluble sugar in both varieties exhibited an upward trend, while the contents of tea polyphenols, phenol ammonia, and total flavonoids showed a downward trend. These results preliminarily reflected the chemical compositional changes in tea plants in response to altitude and underscore the potential significance of genetic background and environmental factors in determining the final quality of tea leaves.
The mineral elements in tea were crucial to its quality, which influenced the intrinsic compounds by activating the expression of related pathways, and their dissolution in the tea soup dominated the balance of flavor (
Bai et al., 2023
; L.
Sun et al., 2023
). As shown in

3.1.2
Catechins, caffeine, and gallic acid composition analysis
Catechins were the main polyphenols in tea and were classified as flavanol compounds. Catechins could be classified into ester type catechins (ETC) and nonester type catechins (NETC) (
Zhang et al., 2019
). ETC was abundant in a large number of hydroxyl groups, which bestowed significant antioxidant properties and various health benefits to tea. Meanwhile, NETC played a crucial role in enhancing the flavor quality of tea soup (
Zhou et al., 2025
). As shown in
Fig. 3
I-J, the ETC content of ZC108 and FY6 was significantly higher than that of NETC (
P
< 0.05), which was consistent with a previous study indicating that catechins were mainly ETC (
Xu et al., 2024
). Under the same altitude range, the ETC, NETC, and total catechins content of ZC108 were all higher than those of FY6. It was speculated that ZC108 possessed a stronger overall antioxidant capacity, a richer array of functional components, and a more pronounced flavor profile. As altitude increased, both varieties exhibited a downward trend in ETC content, NETC content, and total catechins content. This decline could primarily be attributed to the relatively low temperatures in high-altitude regions, which slowed the growth rate of tea trees. Consequently, more carbon sources accumulated were redirected towards nitrogen metabolism pathways, such as amino acid synthesis, resulting in a reduced accumulation of carbon metabolic products, such as catechins (
Shao et al., 2022
).

With increasing altitude, the levels of EC, CG, EGC, C, GCG, and GC in both ZC108 and FY6 exhibited a downward trend, which was consistent with a previous study (

). The epigallocatechin (EGC) content in high-altitude areas was higher than that in low-altitude regions (

).
CAF was the main source of bitterness in tea soup and had a significant effect on refreshing and invigorating the mind, and played a crucial role in both the flavor and physiological activity of tea (
Chu et al., 2023
). As shown in
Fig. 3
K, there was no significant difference in CAF content between ZC108 and FY6 within the same altitude range. However, with increasing altitude, the CAF content of both varieties exhibited a significant upward trend (
P
< 0.05), with CAF content in high-altitude areas being more than 2.2 times greater than those in the low-altitude areas. This phenomenon might be attributed to the intense ultraviolet radiation present in high-altitude environments. Strong ultraviolet rays could enhance the activity of key enzymes, such as xanthine
N
-methyltransferase, in the CAF synthesis pathway, thereby promoting CAF biosynthesis (
Zhu et al., 2023
).
GA was a major phenolic acid in tea leaves and exhibited potent scavenging capacity against •OH and •OOH
−
radicals (
Ge et al., 2021
). As shown in
Fig. 3
L, within the same altitude range, the GA content in FY6 was generally higher than that in ZC108. Furthermore, both varieties exhibited higher GA levels at higher elevations compared to lower elevations. This phenomenon primarily occurred because GA could be incorporated into ETC via galloyltransferase. However, the lower temperatures in high-altitude environments inhibited the activity of this enzyme, hindering the conversion of GA to ETC. Consequently, GA accumulated as a substrate within the metabolic pathway, leading to an increase of its content (
Wei et al., 2025
). This observation was further supported by the experimental results in
Fig. 3
I, which showed lower ETC content at higher elevations and higher ETC content in ZC108.
In summary, the total catechins content, ETC, NETC, EGCG, EC, CG, EGC, GCG contents of ZC108 were generally higher than that of FY6 within the same altitude range. With increasing altitude, the levels of EGCG, EC, EGC, GCG, total catechins, ETC, and NETC in both varieties exhibited a decreasing trend. Combined with the experimental results presented in Section 3.1.1, these chemical component data provide a theoretical basis for the quality advantage of high-altitude tea. Subsequent non-targeted metabolomics analyses will further verify and elucidate the characteristics and patterns of these metabolic changes at a more comprehensive molecular level.

Results of multivariate analysis of UHPLC-Q/TOF-MS-based non-target metabolomics
3.2.1
Non-targeted metabolomics analysis across various cultivars
The metabolic data from a total of 34 samples of FY 6 and ZC108 green tea raw materials were obtained by using UHPLC-Q-TOF/MS. A total of 2881 metabolites were identified, with 1365 metabolites annotated in positive ion mode and 1516 metabolites annotated in negative ion mode (

A). The primary metabolites identified included isoprenoid lipids and carboxylic acids along with their derivatives (
Fig. 4
B). The data were assessed for suitability prior to principal component analysis using the KMO test and Bartlett's test of sphericity. Bartlett's test yielded a chi-square value of 6371.73 (df = 1225,
p
< 0.001). The KMO measure of sampling adequacy was 0.72. These results confirmed that the data were appropriate for further analysis.

These heatmaps were constructed using Euclidean distance and Ward clustering, with the intensity of the colors representing the levels of metabolite expression. As shown in
Fig. 6

Additionally, there were three sugar metabolites and 8 other substances that did not fall into the aforementioned categories. The results indicated that flavonoids, flavonoid glycosides, organic acids, amino acids, and phenolic acids were the predominant non-volatile differential metabolites distinguishing the tea samples from the two varieties, FY6 and ZC108. γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA), L-theanine, and procyanidin B2 3,3′-di-O-gallate exhibited significant differences among the varieties at the same altitude, with the average content in FY6 being higher than that in ZC108. In terms of flavonoids and flavonoid glycosides, the content of myricetin, kaempferol-3-O-rutinoside, and kaempferol was higher in ZC108, FY6 was rich in theaflavin monogallates, theaflavin digallate, isoengeletin, and naringenin. Among flavonoids and flavonoid glycosides, the rutin content in FY6 was more abundant. In other categories,
d

As illustrated in
Fig. 6
B, the primary metabolites identified included flavonoids and flavonoglycans (9 species), phenolic acids (6 species), organic acids (5 species), amino acids (3 species), and sugars (5 species). The hierarchical clustering algorithm grouped substances with similar trends in content changes into a single class, indicating the association of their metabolic pathways and synergistic functions. This analysis further revealed the marker metabolites that were strongly correlated with altitude. Notably, 6-O-beta-D-Fructofuranosyl-
d
-glucose, Apigenin 7-alpha-L-arabinopyranosyl-(1 → 6)-glucoside, Rutin, 6″-acetylononin, Teacarotenetetrol, 9,10,18-triOH-12-octadecenoic acid, and 3-hydroxy-2-octylpentanedioic acid exhibited significantly higher concentrations in samples collected at altitudes of ≥700 m compared to those at <700 m. Additionally, L-Theanine and Dehydroascorbic acid also demonstrated increased accumulation at this altitude, which was hypothesized to contribute to coping with the environmental stresses associated with low temperatures at high altitude (
Li et al., 2022
).
A previous study also found that catechins, EGCG, EGC, GC, C, and chlorogenic acid were more abundant at <700 m, which was correlated with the fact that lower temperatures inhibited the expression of the relevant metabolic pathways (
Xiang et al., 2021
). Kaempferol, 2-hydroxyhexadecanoic acid, uridine diphosphate (UDP), and astragalin exhibited higher concentrations at lower altitudes (< 700 m). To cope with low temperatures and intense UV stress in high-altitude environments, the tea plant synergistically regulated three major metabolic pathways to enhance resilience. In the phenylpropane pathway, low temperature and UV radiation synergistically activated the initiator enzyme PAL, which promoted the accumulation of phenolic acids (e.g., caffeic acid) to scavenge reactive oxygen species and alleviate photo-oxidative damage (
Yu, Zhou, Meng, Zhou, & Xu, 2025
). In the Flavonoid pathway, Although low temperature inhibited the activities of enzymes such as chalcone synthase (CHS) and flavanone 3-hydroxylase (F3H), reducing the synthesis of catechins (e.g., EGC, EGCG), UV radiation specifically induced the expression of FLS (
Yu et al., 2025
). This directed metabolic flow towards flavonols (e.g., rutin), which had UV-shielding functions, resulting in their enrichment in high-altitude samples (
Liu, Gregan, Winefield, & Jordan, 2015
). In the Purine pathway, UV radiation activated the key enzyme tea caffeine synthase (TCS), promoting the accumulation of caffeine, a highly effective antioxidant in leaves, thereby systematically enhancing the tea plant's resistance (
Vieira, Gaspar, & Santos, 2020
).

Analysis of the interaction between cultivars and altitudes on differential metabolites in fresh tea leaves
Based on VIP >1.0 and
P
< 0.05, 50 differential metabolites associated with cultivar and 40 associated with altitude were screened. After removing duplicates, 56 unique metabolites were obtained for subsequent interaction analysis. To evaluate the interaction between cultivar and altitude, a two-way ANOVA was conducted on these 56 metabolites. Subsequent two-way ANOVA of the 56 metabolites for cultivar and altitude interaction identified 31 significant metabolites were shown in Table S2. Coumarin was the most notable for its highly significant interaction (
P
< 0.0001), alongside a significant cultivar main effect (
P
= 0.022) and a non-significant altitude main effect (
P
= 0.103). This interaction corresponded to a reversal in which cultivar had higher coumarin content at different altitudes (
Fig. 7
). Specifically, ZC108 had significantly higher coumarin content than FY6 at low altitudes. This relationship reversed completely at high altitudes, where FY6 content became greater (
Fig. 7
A). This distinct crossover pattern demonstrated that coumarin biosynthesis was co-regulated by genetic background and environmental factors, and that different cultivars employed fundamentally different metabolic strategies in response to environmental stress, thereby establishing the pivotal role of genetic background in modulating the tea plant's metabolic response to altitudinal stress.

3.3.1
Machine learning and biomarker screening utilizing diverse metabolic data from various cultivars
After screening of 50 differential metabolites to distinguish between the two cultivar classes, FY6 and ZC108, machine learning was applied to non-targeted differential metabolomics data to achieve cultivar discrimination. The classification was divided into two categories: FY6 and ZC108. The SVM, RF, and KNN models were trained using 70 % of the data from the measured samples as the training set, while the remaining 30 % of the sample data was utilized as the test set to evaluate the models' performance.

To assess the model's ability to distinguish between positive and negative samples, the AUC was utilized. The closer the AUC was to 1, the stronger the model's classification capability. The ROC curve for the SVM (
Fig. 8
B) exhibited a vertically towards the vicinity of (0,1) rapidly before extending horizontally. Similarly, the ROC curve for the RF model (

In cultivars identification, three models (SVM, RF, KNN) demonstrated strong performance in classifying tea varieties. The accuracy of each model was 100 %, and the AUC values were all 1.00. However, the ROC curves exhibited different shapes, highlighting the variations in their underlying modeling principles. The SVM and RF models could accurately distinguish between the two types of varieties at an early stage, established a clear decision boundary. In contrast, the KNN model's decision-making was more dynamic and dependent on the threshold, resulted in a comparatively weaker ability to make rapid decisions. This indicated that the SVM and RF models outperform the KNN model in this context.
Further analysis through MDA in RF identified 15 potential chemical markers closely associated with the cultivars (
Fig. 9
). A higher score signified that a feature had a greater influence on the model's predictive outcomes, indicating its importance within the model. From a ranking perspective, phenylethanol emerged as the most significant feature for differentiating among the varieties. In a previous study, phenylethanol had been identified as the key aromatic compound in tea, classified as a volatile alcohol (
Zhou et al., 2018
) and was characterized by its significant rosy and sweet fruity aromas. Phenylethanol showed significant variations in volatile metabolites among different varieties of fresh tea leaves (
Fu et al., 2024
), which aligned with our non-targeted metabolomics data that the phenylethanol content in ZC108 was higher than that in FY6. Kaempferol, a flavonoid present in tea, served as a crucial marker of high-quality tea infusion, contributed to astringency and possessed antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties similar to those of quercetin, as well as offered protective effects against liver damage (

). The concentration of kaempferol was closely associated with the tea cultivars; the levels of kaempferol and total flavonols in small-leaf tea (

) were significantly higher than those in the Assam cultivars (var. assamica) and hybrid cultivars (ssp. lasiocalyx) (

). In our study, we also observed that at <700 m, the kaempferol content in ZC108 was elevated. The key variables identified through random forest modeling were closely associated with the different varieties, revealing significant differences between ZC108 and FY6. This indicated that the highly ranked variables were the most critical factors in differentiating the sources of various green tea varieties.

This indicated that the metabolites in green tea from varying altitudes could serve as a crucial basis for determining altitude.

Conclusion
The present study systematically investigated the effects of cultivar and altitude on tea quality using non-targeted metabolomics and machine learning approaches. The results demonstrated that cultivar was the primary factor influencing the tea quality, exerting a greater effect than altitude. The ZC108 exhibited significantly higher levels of multiple taste-related compounds compared to FY6. With increasing elevation, the contents of tea polyphenols, amino acids, and various secondary metabolites decreased, whereas the activities of phenylpropanoid, purine, and flavonoid metabolic pathways were enhanced. High-accuracy discrimination of cultivar and altitude was achieved using SVM/RF/KNN models. This study confirmed that metabolomics combined with machine learning can effectively trace the cultivar and geographical origin of tea. Future work should expand the sample size, integrate volatile metabolite data, and further explore the relationship between metabolites and sensory quality.
